definition: A positively charged ion, formed when an atom, usually of a metal, loses one or more electrons, such as $\ce{Na^+}$ or $\ce{Fe^3+}$.
A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom, usually of a non-metal, gains one or more electrons, such as $\ce{Cl^-}$ or $\ce{O^2-}$.
An ion made of two or more covalently bonded atoms that carries an overall charge and stays together as a unit, such as $\ce{NH4^+}$ or $\ce{SO4^2-}$.
The electrostatic attraction between positive ions and negative ions; it acts equally in all directions, holding the ions in a lattice.
The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is separated into its gaseous ions; it is always positive and is larger for ions with higher charges and smaller radii.
The radius of an ion; a cation is smaller than its atom and an anion is larger than its atom.
The ability of a substance to carry an electric current, which needs charged particles free to move, such as ions in a molten or dissolved ionic compound, or delocalized electrons in a metal.
The amount of a substance that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a stated temperature; ionic compounds are often soluble in water but not in non-polar solvents.
